source.title: Configuration-to-Performance Scaling Law with Neural Ansatz
source.authors: Hua-Qing Zhang; Kai-Yue Wen; Teng-Yu Ma

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Fits a Chinchilla-form power-law baseline using training runs and evaluates its predictions of held-out pretraining losses, including runs with larger model sizes. This tests the loss-prediction behavior of the scaling-law baseline, though it is not a replication of the original studies' full experimental setups.
record.gate_note: The paper also evaluates NCPL, XGBoost, loss-curve prediction, and learning-rate/batch-size selection. Those results do not directly test the listed versions about power-law loss scaling, power-law extrapolation, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, architecture sensitivity, other modalities, or downstream task performance. The power-law baseline is reported in Table 1; only its final-loss prediction metrics are recorded here. The authors state that NCPL generalizes to up to 10× more compute than any training run, but that is a claim about NCPL, not the power-law baseline.
record.test_reason: The Chinchilla law is a residual baseline and comparison point for the authors' NCPL predictor. It is fit on the best run per (N,D) among models of at most 430M parameters. It is then scored against all held-out runs, including deliberately suboptimal hyperparameter settings. Its MAE, RMSE and Spearman values therefore mostly measure hyperparameter-induced spread, which a configuration-agnostic law cannot capture by design. They do not show whether loss follows a power law under well-tuned conditions, or whether it extrapolates over orders of magnitude. The OOD split reaches about 1.2B parameters (≤10× compute), not orders of magnitude. No exponents, compute-optimal split, architecture, modality or downstream results are reported for the law.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. NCPL predicts configuration-dependent final loss with 20-40% lower MAE than the Chinchilla baseline. It generalizes to runs with up to 10× more compute, supports joint learning-rate/batch-size tuning, and predicts loss curves. The authors call it a proof of concept limited by available logs.
record.recipe_differences: The paper fits the Chinchilla-law form on selected training runs and evaluates held-out predictions using Marin and StepLaw logs. It does not reproduce the original studies' full experiments or test their compute-optimal parameter/token allocation conclusions; its primary method is a neural configuration-to-performance predictor.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction performance differs by dataset and split. The paper reports that configuration-aware NCPL outperforms the configuration-agnostic Chinchilla baseline; the OOD split is defined by model sizes larger than 430M parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed (N,D), final pretraining loss varies substantially with learning rate, batch size, optimizer and weight decay. A Chinchilla law in N and D alone cannot capture this spread; a configuration-aware predictor cuts MAE by 20-40%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining loss at fixed parameters and tokens depends materially on training hyperparameters and optimizer, beyond the N,D power law.

record.problems: The authors state that training data include models only up to 430M parameters and OOD validation models at most 1.2B parameters, and note limited configuration diversity and only two pretraining datasets. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the prediction metrics. The claimed 10× compute extrapolation is for NCPL rather than the Chinchilla-law baseline.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant Chinchilla-law final-loss prediction metrics from Table 1 were left out.

untested.parts: Not tested: power-law loss on well-tuned runs, with fitted exponents, over several orders of magnitude.
Not tested: extrapolation over orders of magnitude. The OOD gap is about 3× in parameters and up to 10× in compute, and is scored against non-optimal runs.
Not tested: architecture shape at fixed N.
Not tested: other modalities or training regimes.
Not tested: dependence of exponents or compute-optimal split on fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Appendix B.1 says, qualitatively, that a Chinchilla baseline fit on ≤430M models overpredicts loss at N≈1073M. This hints at an extrapolation limit for V2, but no number is given and the range is far below orders of magnitude, so no verdict is assigned. The reader's limits_scope labels are dropped: the rows measure configuration spread rather than the law.

versions.untested_parts: The study evaluates a fitted Chinchilla-form law on held-out pretraining losses, but does not isolate parameter, token, and compute scaling, report fitted exponents, or establish power-law behavior over several orders of magnitude with the other quantities non-bottlenecking.

The power-law baseline is tested on the reported held-out splits, but the text does not establish that the baseline predicts runs orders of magnitude larger. The up-to-10× compute extrapolation claim is for NCPL.
No test of compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as a function of compute. Learning-rate and batch-size selection is not this version.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No experiments in other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer.

The study discusses configuration dependence and fits a baseline, but does not test dependence of power-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, nor test whether curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.operation_detail: Fit the Chinchilla-law form on the training set and evaluate final-loss predictions on held-out runs.
rows.note: The reported error measures prediction against held-out run losses; it does not itself identify which scaling axis accounts for the error.
rows.check: Baseline error against runs with varied hyperparameters. The error mixes configuration spread with any power-law misfit. This is a comparison with the study's own method, not a test of V1/V2.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Held-out Marin and StepLaw runs with varying training configurations
reader_labels.reason: The Chinchilla-law baseline is evaluated on these runs, but the study emphasizes that configuration-agnostic predictions are less accurate than configuration-aware predictions; the experiment does not establish the law under optimally tuned, non-bottlenecking conditions. Rows r1-r12.

reader_labels.reason: The fitted Chinchilla baseline has reported OOD prediction metrics, but the tested size range is limited and the paper's stated up-to-10× compute generalization result applies to NCPL, not this power-law baseline. Rows r4-r6 and r10-r12.
